analysis.one_liner: Replaces the Medicare catastrophic surtax on wealthier seniors with a higher top income tax rate.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on June 6, 1989 and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The Medicare Catastrophic Coverage Act of 1988 added prescription drug coverage and caps on out-of-pocket medical costs for seniors, financed partly by a surtax that rose with a senior's income tax bill — so better-off seniors paid far more for benefits everyone received. Public opposition from seniors was fierce. This bill would have kept the benefits, repealed the surtax, and instead paid for the program by making the 33% top income tax rate apply to all high incomes, ending the phase-out of the 15% rate and personal exemptions, and setting a 28% maximum capital gains rate [S2][S3]. It died in committee without ever reaching a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries would keep the 1988 law's catastrophic hospital and doctor benefits and new drug coverage, while no longer paying the income-based surtax. Wealthier taxpayers above roughly the $71,900 top bracket threshold would bear more of the cost through the extended 33% rate, though they would also benefit from the 28% capital gains cap.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the supplemental Medicare premium — the surtax added by the 1988 catastrophic law that scaled with each senior's income tax liability — retroactive to taxable years after 1988 [S2][S3].

Keeps the catastrophic coverage and prescription drug benefits in place by appropriating their costs to the Hospital Insurance, Supplementary Medical Insurance, and Catastrophic Drug trust funds, funded from general receipts [S2][S3].

Pays for the benefits by extending the 33% individual income tax rate to all income above the top bracket threshold and repealing the phase-out of the 15% rate and personal exemptions, shifting the burden toward the highest earners [S2][S3].
Retains modest monthly premiums on beneficiaries — $4.00 per month for catastrophic coverage in 1989, rising over time, with drug premiums starting in 1991 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-income taxpayers, whose top-bracket income would be taxed at 33% with no phase-out of the 15% rate or personal exemptions, and to a lesser extent Medicare beneficiaries, who would continue paying monthly catastrophic and drug premiums that rise through 1993 and beyond.

drawbacks.text: Beneficiaries would still owe monthly premiums: the bill keeps a catastrophic coverage premium starting at $4.00 per month in 1989 and rising to $7.18 by 1993, plus prescription drug premiums beginning in 1991, with premiums after 1993 tied to estimated per-capita program costs [S3].

Raising the top individual rate to 33% on all income above the top threshold would be a substantial tax increase on the highest earners, and the bill's 28% cap on capital gains gives investors a partial offset that makes the financing mix less progressive [S3].

Funding the program from general receipts through annual appropriations to the trust funds makes the benefits dependent on future Congresses continuing to fund them, unlike the 1988 law's dedicated premium and surtax financing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade-off is straightforward: seniors keep new catastrophic and drug benefits and stop paying a surtax that scaled with income tax liability, while the cost moves to the general taxpayer through a higher top rate. The main weaknesses are that beneficiaries still pay premiums that grow over time, and that general-receipt financing is less secure than dedicated premiums — a real concern, since Congress ultimately chose to repeal the benefits entirely rather than restructure the financing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on June 6, 1989, got no hearing, markup, or vote, and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 1991 — and by then Congress had instead voted to repeal the entire 1988 catastrophic law.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin introduced the bill on June 6, 1989, for himself and Sens. Levin and Metzenbaum; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S1][S3][S5].
The Finance Committee took no further action — the bill's complete action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action after the referral [S5].
The bill attracted only two cosponsors in the Senate, both Democrats, and never left committee before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy seniors and high-income taxpayers came out ahead: rather than adopting this bill's alternative financing, Congress repealed the 1988 catastrophic law outright in late 1989, eliminating the surtax the bill targeted — but seniors also lost the drug coverage and out-of-pocket caps the law had promised, and top earners avoided the 33% rate extension the bill would have imposed.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to replace the catastrophic surtax with a 33% top income tax rate to fund the benefits

for.name: Sens. Carl Levin and Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only two cosponsors

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 6, 1989 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died there [S5]

against.name: President George H.W. Bush and congressional leaders
against.what_they_did: Backed repeal of the entire Medicare Catastrophic Coverage Act in late 1989 rather than an alternative financing fix, which succeeded as P.L. 101-234 and removed the reason for the bill

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all three sponsors were Senate Democrats, and the record shows no Republican support or opposition on the bill itself.

industries.industry: High-income households (incomes above roughly the $71,900 top bracket)
industries.note: The bill would have taxed all income above the top bracket threshold at 33% and repealed the phase-out of the 15% rate and personal exemptions, raising taxes on the highest earners to fund seniors' benefits. Avoiding this — and ultimately repealing the whole 1988 law — left them better off at the cost of the new benefits.

Beneficiaries would keep catastrophic hospital and doctor benefits and new drug coverage while shedding the surtax, retaining only modest monthly premiums. This group is a concentrated constituency rather than an industry, but it is the bill's central beneficiary.

The bill sets a 28% maximum capital gains rate, a modest benefit for investors that slightly offsets the progressive financing behind the benefits and makes the overall tax package less redistributive.
